title: Scam Offensives in Southeast Asia: Comparing Beijing's and Washington's Strategies and Assessing Opportunities for Coordination
text:
Executive Summary

Disrupting Asia’s cyber scam industry, which is valued at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion annually, presents a rare point of mutual interest for the United States and China. Both Chinese and American citizens are both primary targets of complex online fraud schemes run predominantly out of Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos. To identify where opportunities for cooperation on addressing the issue exist for the United States and China, this paper examines the nature of Beijing's crackdowns on cyber scam operations in Southeast Asia, when Beijing chooses to act, and how. It identifies three core factors driving Chinese action: domestic pressure, reputational damage, and national security concerns. Where these factors converge, as in Myanmar, Beijing has acted swiftly and forcefully. Where reputational pressure collides with countervailing strategic interests, as in Cambodia, Beijing's pressure has been delayed but has grown over time. And where none of the three factors materially apply, as in Laos, Beijing has yet to move against major actors. When Beijing does act, it leverages bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral frameworks to conduct joint operations and intelligence gathering with its Southeast Asian partners. Framed under China’s Global Security Initiative (GSI), these mechanisms have broadened the country’s security relationships across the region—although partner states have not always welcomed Beijing's inroads.As Beijing conducted raids against scam centers in Myanmar, the industry began redirecting its targeting toward the West: American losses to China-linked criminal groups grew to $10 billion per year by 2024. Washington has responded with a cross-departmental campaign of sanctions, indictments, asset seizures, and takedowns of scam-enabling online infrastructure. Still, the U.S. response is hampered by limited operational capacity on the ground in Southeast Asia and the "whack-a-mole" nature of the industry.Concerns about China’s GSI expansion, intelligence sharing sensitivities, host-state political economies, and Beijing’s treatment of trafficked workers are substantial obstacles that stand in the way of U.S.-China cooperation on this issue. Still, bounded cooperation has the potential to serve the interests of both Beijing and Washington. There appears to be recognition of this on the ministerial level: FBI Director Kash Patel has traveled to Beijing twice in the past year to discuss expanding coordination on tackling cyber scams with China, alongside several other forms of transnational crime. In April, the United States, China, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates organized a joint raid on scam centers in Dubai; however, misaligned incentives and strategic distrust have thus far stood in the way of further law enforcement coordination between Beijing and Washington.In support of future law enforcement coordination between China and the United States that takes into account existing obstacles rather than ignoring them, this paper draws on an understanding of Beijing’s cyber scam offensive in Southeast Asia to propose the following recommendations for how Washington could pursue tactical and bounded coordination on the issue:Push for leader-to-leader engagement, drawing on lessons from the fentanyl negotiations;Utilize third countries to mediate and coordinate joint raids and intelligence sharing;Approach Beijing with intelligence-backed asks;Leverage existing channels to facilitate financial intelligence sharing; andContinue using sanctions and indictments to incentivize Beijing to recall key actors.

State of the Scam Industry

In 2025, Americans lost $17.6 billion to cyber-enabled fraud, with most of that money going to Chinese-linked transnational crime groups operating industrial-scale illegal gambling and scamming operations out of Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia. “Pig butchering,” or sha-zhu-pan in Mandarin, is one of the techniques used by these criminal groups to scam victims out of their life savings: scammers form relationships with unsuspecting individuals over text or social media, earn their trust, convince them to invest in fraudulent schemes, and then cut contact when victims try to withdraw their investments. Those on the other side of the screen are often victims of this industry themselves, trafficked into scam centers by the prospect of high-paying jobs and abused when they fail to meet quotas. Experts suggest that upwards of 300,000 individuals have been trafficked into centers across Mekong Southeast Asia to run these scams from across Asia and as far away as Western Africa.Behind Southeast Asia’s cyber scam centers are criminal syndicates that were pushed out of China during a series of anti-corruption and anti-crime crackdowns that President Xi Jinping instituted after assuming office in 2012. These crackdowns targeted China’s underground gambling market leading syndicates to move abroad—including to Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos—where Chinese investments were welcomed and governance was thin. When the number of visitors to the casinos they set up in Southeast Asia dropped during the Covid-19 pandemic, Chinese criminal syndicates capitalized on the growing world of online connection and pivoted to focusing on "pig-butchering" and other online fraud scams, expanding their reach far beyond the region and multiplying their profits.Since the pandemic, China-linked criminal syndicates have become deeply embedded in the political economies of Southeast Asia, forming concentrated hubs of illicit activity that function outside of the bounds of state regulatory controls. In Cambodia, criminal operators enjoy elite protection from the highest levels of the Cambodian government. In Myanmar, scam centers operate across both junta and ethnic armed groups (EAO) controlled jurisdictions, benefiting from widespread governance gaps and the reliance of armed actors on the industry to help fund the civil war. In Laos, syndicates have implanted themselves in special economic zones with weak law enforcement, bolstered by support from leading political figures.Prior to 2023, the primary targets of scam operations were Chinese nationals, causing social instability and economic struggles that netizens protested online. In 2021, China introduced a series of laws that cracked down on telecom fraud and banned cryptocurrency. The government began a robust public awareness campaign and used scare tactics to convince Chinese nationals not to travel to Southeast Asia. That year, Chinese nationals lost $5.5 billion to cyber fraud. By 2023, that amount ballooned to an estimated $33.8 billion, prompting the first of many major joint operations between the Chinese Ministry of Public Security (MPS) and Myanmar’s military junta to capture and repatriate scammers along their shared border. By January 2024, Chinese police announced they had reduced online fraud against Chinese citizens by 28.6% since the previous August.But China’s push did not eradicate the threat of scam centers—instead, scammers recalibrated their operations to target Western victims. Although the Chinese government reported a decrease in losses to online scams in 2024, the United States witnessed a 66% increase as American losses jumped to $10 billion that year alone. Sha-yang-pan, or “foreigner butchering,” has since emerged as a Mandarin term used to describe this kind of fraud directed at non-Chinese victims. In response, the U.S. government began making the first moves in its anti-scam offensive by September 2024, though the efforts did not ramp up until a year later.In October 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) issued an indictment against Fujian-born and Cambodia-naturalized Chen Zhi, CEO of the Prince Group, a Cambodian conglomerate that U.S. prosecutors described as the hub of a massive global scam, gambling, and illicit finance network. American authorities then designated the Prince Group as a transnational criminal organization, issued joint sanctions with the United Kingdom against 117 actors in Chen’s network, and seized nearly $15 billion in assets connected to his operations—the largest criminal asset seizure in history. In January 2026, Chen was extradited to China, following what the Cambodian government described as an arrest request from Chinese authorities and follow-through investigations conducted by relevant Cambodian agencies.The arrest of Chen Zhi occurred as the U.S. and Chinese governments had independently put pressure on Cambodia to crack down on its cybercrime industry, which is estimated to bring in as much as $19 billion annually, equivalent to nearly 40% of the country’s formal GDP. Following Chen Zhi’s extradition to China, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet pledged to “clean up” online scamming and eradicate all scam centers by the end of April 2026. The Cambodian government claims to have cracked down on 488 scam locations between January 1 and June 25, 2026, and deported nearly 16,000 people linked to scam operations. However, according to a recent study by Amnesty International, more than 70% of the scam compounds they tracked were essentially bypassed and remain operational. Politically connected high-level operators have escaped accountability and have relocated their operations within the Mekong region, Timor-Leste, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, and beyond.Addressing the scam epidemic will require accountability for operators at the highest levels, especially as the operations of low-level scammers are increasingly being turbocharged by artificial intelligence (AI). Since Chen Zhi’s indictment, the United States has sanctioned organizations and individuals embedded in cyber scam networks, seized online platforms used for cryptocurrency laundering, and recovered stolen funds. However, American officials have admitted one of the biggest barriers to combating scam centers in Southeast Asia is that any arrest is conditional on local cooperation. By wielding sanctions and executing asset seizures Washington can exhibit economic leverage, but it is Beijing that ultimately has both the ability and leverage needed to arrest many of the key actors involved. Chen’s arrest illustrates what becomes possible when the United States and China wield parallel pressure, altering the political expendability of a protected actor and triggering a real yet selective crackdown by the Cambodian government on the industry.While Chen Zhi’s sanctions and arrest unfolded in parallel but uncoordinated tracks, a real joint effort occurred in April when the United States and China joined with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Thailand for a joint raid on scam centers in Dubai, arresting 276 telecom fraud suspects and dismantling fraud dens. The timing of the Dubai joint raid in April, just two weeks before Trump and Xi met in Beijing, was not incidental—giving it the green light was a way for both sides to express goodwill going into the summit. The groundwork for the operation was likely laid when FBI Director Kash Patel travelled to Beijing in November to meet with China’s vice minister of public security, opening direct lines of communication with the first director-level visit since 2016. While no readout of the meeting is publicly available, government officials familiar with the matter have confirmed that scam centers were discussed.This instance of coordination is the exception, not the rule. Deep political distrust and misaligned incentives continue to obstruct sustained bilateral coordination on cyber scam enforcement by the United States and China. Still, there appears to be interest in further cooperation at a ministerial level: in a July 2026 meeting, Patel and China’s Minister of Public Security Wang Xiaohong agreed to expand cooperation on joint raids against scam centers. To assess the viability of future bilateral coordination on this issue, this paper examines the nature of China’s crackdown on Southeast Asia’s scam economy, determines where incentives align and diverge for Washington and Beijing, identifies where coordination is politically realistic, and offers recommendations for how American policymakers can further pursue bounded tactical coordination with China.

China's Cyber Scam Offensive in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos

While China has made a concerted effort to combat cyber scams in Southeast Asia since 2023, enforcement has been selective and interest-contingent, and it has not fundamentally disrupted the industry. This section unpacks how the Chinese government has orchestrated its crackdowns on cyber scam operations in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos—examining when Beijing chooses to act and through which mechanisms when it does.MyanmarNodes of Chinese-linked illegal activity in Myanmar developed along Myanmar’s border with China in the late 1990s to early 2000s and then along the border with Thailand between 2017 and 2021. These centers began running gambling operations across the region but pivoted to “pig-butchering” scams during Covid-19. According to the U.S. Institute of Peace’s 2024 study “Transnational Crime in Southeast Asia,” there were more than 100 scamming enclaves along Myanmar’s Chinese border and more than 30 along its Thai border by 2023.As China reopened its borders in 2023, public alarm rose over a series of widely publicized cases of Chinese nationals either scammed or kidnapped in Myanmar, and the Chinese government began pressuring Myanmar’s junta to close the scam centers. In May, then Chinese Foreign Minister Qin Gang visited Naypyidaw for the first high-level visit to Myanmar since the coup and urged junta leader Ming Aung Hlaing to crack down on cross-border telecom fraud. In August, officials from Myanmar and China reactivated a bilateral channel for information sharing related to border safety. In September, China moved from issuing warnings and threats to taking direct action against the scam operations: MPS and the junta launched a joint operation that brought down 11 scam dens in northern Myanmar. China’s MPS also began ad hoc coordination with Myanmar’s EAOs to conduct raids of scam compounds. In the first week of September, coordination between China’s MPS and the United Wa State Army resulted in the repatriation of 1,207 fraud suspects to China.Frustrated with what they viewed as insufficient cooperation from the junta, in October China tacitly greenlit a major operation against the Myanmar military by a coalition of EAOs under Beijing’s influence. Known as the Three Brotherhood Alliance, the coalition sought to gain control of the Kokang region and key military outposts in the northern Shan state along the Chinese border. It announced at the outset of the offensive, known as Operation 1027, that eliminating scam centers was a central objective, likely in part to gain the green light of the Chinese government. By the end of 2023, the Chinese government announced that more than 41,000 scam suspects had been handed over from authorities in northern Myanmar as part of Operation 1027. Among these actors were members of the Ming and Bai families, two of the notorious “Four Families” that have run criminal activities in Myanmar since the early 2000s. The penalties for these actors were harsh: in early 2026, Chinese courts carried out the executions of eleven members of the Ming family criminal group and four members of the Bai family criminal group.After Operation 1027, both the focal geography and strategy underpinning China’s operations in Myanmar shifted. Following the enhanced crackdowns on centers along Myanmar’s border with China, scam operators began moving operations to Myawaddy and Shwe Kokko in Kayin State along the Myanmar-Thailand border. When the Three Brotherhood Alliance broke a Chinese-brokered ceasefire in June 2024, Beijing intensified cooperation with the junta to crack down on scam centers, and by the end of 2025, Chinese authorities and the junta announced that they had jointly arrested more than 57,000 Chinese nationals for their participation in cyber scams since 2023.CambodiaBy 2017, Sihanoukville, Cambodia, had emerged as an epicenter of Chinese criminal activity as real estate developers sought to capitalize on the wave of gambling operations expelled from China during Xi’s anti-crime push. Relaxed regulations and a surge in Chinese immigration led to a rise in incidents involving Chinese gangs, which prompted then Prime Minister Hun Sen to ban online gambling in 2019—a move that experts have attributed in part to pressure from Beijing to clean up corruption in China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). In August 2019, China and Cambodia opened a Law Enforcement Cooperation Office in Phnom Penh, the first such bilateral office set up by China overseas.Once gambling was outlawed in Cambodia and Covid-19 disrupted the flow of Chinese foot traffic into casinos, Sihanoukville’s criminal syndicates pivoted, transforming the existing physical and financial gambling infrastructure into hubs for cyber scam operations. Only operations run by politically connected elites had the cover and resources to survive this period of instability; control over Cambodia’s scam industry was consolidated into the hands of actors who had connections up to the highest levels of Cambodia’s government, such as Chen Zhi, who served as an advisor to Hun Sen and later his son Hun Manet. Many Chinese nationals such as Chen paid for Cambodian citizenship to reduce extradition risk and deepen their integration into local protection networks.By 2022, China raised pressure on the Cambodian government through bilateral channels, including to Hun Sen himself, leading Cambodia’s police to raid a number of scam centers across the country, although mostly in Sihanoukville, for the first time. Many owners were tipped off ahead of time and bussed their workers into the countryside, so when police arrived there was no one to arrest. The majority of raided compounds reopened just two months later, and no charges were filed against syndicates or owners. This dynamic repeated in subsequent cosmetic crackdowns, including a series of joint Chinese-Cambodian raids in early 2024 that led to the repatriation of 680 scam and gambling suspects to China. Still, Phnom Penh pushed back on Chinese state–endorsed efforts to raise awareness of the cybercrime industry in Cambodia, including banning screenings of the Chinese movie No More Bets, a thriller about a scam center in a lawless and corrupt country conspicuously similar to Cambodia.While the Chinese government has brought up the issue of cyber scams in bilateral channels for years, it has only been within the past year that senior Chinese officials have noted Cambodia’s cyber scam industry as a block in the bilateral relationship. This rhetoric and the extradition of several key actors, starting with Chen Zhi, played a part in catalyzing the Cambodian government to begin its crackdown on scam centers in February 2026.LaosSince the launch of the BRI in 2021, Laos has been a key hub for Chinese infrastructure development, particularly in the form of Chinese-operated special economic zones (SEZs). Among these SEZs, the Golden Triangle SEZ (GTSEZ) has gained a reputation for money laundering, casinos, drugs, prostitution, and now scams. It is operated by Zhao Wei, a Chinese transnational criminal who was sanctioned by the United States in 2018 for drug, wildlife, and human trafficking. Scam operations began to proliferate into the GTSEZ following China’s 2023 crackdowns in Myanmar; however, given Zhao’s close ties to the Laotian government and Vientiane's interest in some of the legitimate operations in the GTSEZ, the government not only lacked the political will to address scam centers but also had reason to endorse them.Rising international coverage of the scam industry and pressure from Beijing led the Lao government to call for its complete eradication by the end of August 2024. As a result, Lao and Chinese authorities carried out nine raids, arresting and deporting 1,389 scammers, 1,211 of whom were Chinese. As in Cambodia, these crackdowns were largely performative, as Lao police are suspected of giving scam center owners advance notice, allowing operators to hide incriminating materials before raids.1 These raids also encouraged operations to disperse beyond SEZs and across the rest of the country in recent years, particularly in central Laos and around Vientiane.As Cambodia has cracked down on its scam ecosystem over the past six months, numerous syndicates have moved operations to Laos, sparking a series of raids led by Lao police in May and June that led to the arrest of more than 1,000 scammers. The recent crackdown points to waning Chinese tolerance toward Zhao Wei and his operations, but Beijing has yet to flex its diplomatic muscle and take serious action against him and his enterprises, as they have done in Cambodia and Myanmar. Recent field research by Jason Tower, senior expert at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Crime, suggests that, as of May 2026, between 30,000 and 35,000 scammers may still be working within the Golden Triangle Economic Zone.2

When China Acts—And When It Does Not

Why has China cracked down heavily in Myanmar, waited to apply pressure on Cambodia, and done comparatively less in Laos? The pattern is explained by three factors that determine the direction and velocity of China’s anti-scam offensive: the expression of domestic discontent, reputational damage to China’s image and its Belt and Road Initiative, and the geographic proximity of scam operations to Chinese territory. Where these factors converge, as in Myanmar, Beijing has acted swiftly and forcefully. Where reputational pressure collides with countervailing strategic interests, as in Cambodia, pressure from Beijing was delayed but grew over time. And where none of the three factors applies in a significant way, as in Laos, Beijing has yet to pursue major actors.Myanmar is where all three drivers converge. By 2022, Chinese social media was flush with stories of Chinese nationals trafficked across the border into Myanmar and complaints about Beijing's failure to help scam victims recover lost funds. Responding to heightened domestic discontent, in 2023 the Chinese government initiated direct involvement in crackdown efforts in Myanmar, televising repatriations of criminals and reporting on the number of scammers who were intercepted during raids. Around the same time, international organizations and media began to link BRI investments in Myanmar with human trafficking and cyber scams run by China-linked transnational criminal groups.Another wave of Chinese action in Myanmar followed the high-profile 2025 abduction of Chinese actor Wang Xing from Mae Sot, Thailand. As Wang’s girlfriend’s social media posts about his abduction went viral, more than 1,800 other Chinese nationals capitalized on attention to the issue, posting demands for the Chinese government to help rescue relatives trafficked into Myanmar’s scam centers. In response, MPS announced that China would launch international law enforcement cooperation to “relentlessly pursue and crack down” on the strongholds of overseas gangs. By July, the Chinese government confirmed that joint operations had resulted in the repatriation of more than 5,400 Chinese nationals involved in fraud in the Myawaddy area. Geography amplified pressure on the Chinese government to act: Myanmar’s scam centers sit near China’s border, posing an immediate threat to Chinese domestic security interests in a way that operations in Cambodia and Laos do not. Public anger and border security concerns pointed in the same direction, and Beijing’s response was correspondingly robust.In Cambodia, the primary catalyst for Chinese action has been reputational damage. Xi has made cultivating favorable international perceptions of China central to his national security strategy, recognizing that crime and corruption along the Belt and Road Initiative degrades China’s desired image as a responsible development partner. By 2019, the proliferation of crime in Sihanoukville had done exactly that, thus instigating China’s response to gambling. International media coverage of China-linked scam syndicates operating in Cambodia had a similar effect by late 2024, leading the Chinese government to press harder in bilateral channels. However, it was only after the U.S. high-profile 2025 indictment of Chen Zhi and joint U.S.-UK sanctions against his Prince Group that China publicly called for Chen’s arrest and extradition, even though Beijing launched a police investigation into Chen in 2020. This has led experts to suggest that it was the indictment and sanctions that finally triggered Beijing to act.This selective tolerance of scam-linked actors can be credited in part to the relationship between Cambodia’s ruling elites and the scam industry. Because Phnom Penh is China’s most reliable geostrategic and economic partner in Southeast Asia, Beijing has seemed to have a higher tolerance for the behavior of actors connected to the Cambodian government. Chinese officials have reported seeking Chen’s extradition years before 2025, but those efforts appear to have been constrained by competing interests within Beijing to maintain a strategic relationship with Phnom Penh; analysts cite China’s demonstrated ability to secure the extradition of its nationals abroad as evidence that if Beijing wanted to move in on Chen, it could have. It was only when international coverage built and the U.S. indictment was issued that Cambodia moved in on Chen and set into motion a series of other high-level extraditions, including Chen’s associates Li Xiong in April and Liu Ren in June. While neither of these actors was specifically sanctioned by the United States, their Prince Group subsidiary companies, Huione and Jin Bei, were, which may have influenced China’s decision to extradite them specifically.Laos is an example of what happens when none of the three drivers is present in a major way: the GTSEZ lacks proximity to the Chinese border, Laos’s scam industry has received comparatively less coverage in both China and the West, and scam boss Zhao Wei has not yet been the subject of an enforcement action on the scale of the Chen Zhi indictment. Zhao’s work has also, in some cases, intersected with Chinese state priorities, which has likely bought him a level of leniency from law enforcement. Decorated for his “development” work by the Lao government, Zhao leveraged the Belt and Road Initiative to add a veneer of legitimacy to his operations in the GTSEZ. He has also expressed support for the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and has party-state ties dating back to his role as founding chair of the Macau ASEAN Chamber of Commerce in the 1990s. The fact that China has, as far as it is publicly known, not put pressure on the Lao government to allow for the arrest and extradition of Zhao can be attributed to a combination of Zhao’s relationships within the Chinese party state and with the Lao government; Beijing’s interest in some of the legitimate operations coming out of the GTSEZ; and, as mentioned previously, the lack of immediate threat that Zhao’s operations pose to Chinese national security interests. Taken together, the divergent fates of Chen Zhi and Zhao Wei reveal a key trend: Beijing has historically been agnostic toward how actors that support the CCP pursue what they claim are national interests abroad, until they are perceived by Beijing as harming Chinese citizens and China’s reputation.Given the connections of actors such as Zhao Wei to parts of the CCP, inquiries have been made into the degree of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) state complicity within the scam industry. In May 2026, the U.S. Select Committee on China released a report in which the committee concluded that even though there was no top-down command of the scam industry from Beijing, “PRC-origin criminal networks and CCP-linked actors have repeatedly benefited from systems of selective enforcement, political protection, illicit finance, and opaque infrastructure.” The report singles out Chen as a case of fragmented interests within the Chinese state, noting that interviews with PRC officials dating back years suggest that different parts of the Chinese government had conflicting aims relative to Chen and the Prince Group. Even after the Chinese government opened an investigation into him in 2020, a central Chinese state-owned enterprise (SOE) subsidiary (China Construction Fourth Engineering Division) constructed major Prince Group assets in Cambodia.The Select Committee Report concluded that Chen’s connections within the party-state do not point to centralized direction from the Chinese government but rather selective screening and corruption that are prevalent across China’s BRI. While Chen worked with SOEs to build his scam compounds, his case did not indicate high-level conspiracy in Beijing behind Chinese criminal groups in Southeast Asia. The Chinese state is not a monolith, and different actors in the vast bureaucracy hold different interests, creating some of the conditions needed for the scam industry to proliferate and limiting the extent of China’s crackdown on Southeast Asia’s scam economy. Understanding these nuances is a precondition for any future coordination between Washington and Beijing on this issue.

Beijing's Global Security Initiative Expands in the Mekong

The expansion of Chinese anti-scam efforts in Southeast Asia and, consequently, the expansion of the Chinese security state have marked a pivot away from Beijing’s long-standing policy of noninterference in the affairs of other countries. With the launch of the Global Security Initiative (GSI) in April 2022, Xi institutionalized a framework for reshaping global security norms and structures to give China an advantage in securing its overseas security and economic interests. China has explicitly linked the involvement of its police in cracking down on online scams as part of the GSI, and it has primarily leveraged joint law enforcement cooperation frameworks with countries across Mekong Southeast Asia to do so.The Lancang-Mekong Integrated Law Enforcement and Security Cooperation Center (LMLECC), established in Kunming, China, in 2017, has become the principal channel since 2023 for joint operations, intelligence sharing, repatriations, and targeted raids carried out by China, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam. In 2024, the LMLECC organized Operation SEAGULL, which coordinated law enforcement from six countries resulting in, according to Chinese state media, more than 160 cases cracked, more than 70,000 criminal suspects arrested, and more than 160 trafficking victims rescued, largely along the China-Myanmar border. After China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged ASEAN diplomats in January 2025 to take strong measures against online gambling and fraud operations, LMLECC members agreed to launch Operation SEAGULL II, mobilizing Chinese, Thai, and junta police forces to address scam operations along the Myanmar-Thailand border.Following its pattern of advancing issue-based frameworks to address regional security concerns, China introduced two multilateral frameworks alongside LMLECC to increase its police presence in the Mekong. In August 2023, China, Thailand, Myanmar, and Laos established a dedicated anti-scam operation supported by a coordination center in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Then, alongside the launch of Operation SEAGULL II, the Myanmar-Thailand-China trilateral task force was created. By March 2026, Beijing announced that more than 1,500 scamming suspects from Myawaddy, Myanmar, had been repatriated to China since the launch of the trilateral mechanism.Bilateral frameworks also laid the groundwork for Chinese operations and intelligence sharing with countries throughout Southeast Asia. Conversely, China has leveraged the scam epidemic to strengthen these bilateral relationships: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Thailand accounted for 26 of the 192 bilateral security meetings held by MPS between mid-2022 and mid-2025. With these four countries, geography has played a key role in shaping the degree to which Beijing has been able to secure law enforcement cooperation. In Myanmar, Beijing holds significant leverage over the EAOs operating near the Chinese border, which it has exercised to keep border regions stable and trade flowing. Its control over water, internet access, and the flow of goods into northern Myanmar has led these groups to occasionally frame their own interests to align with Beijing's. The Three Brotherhood Alliance did exactly this with Operation 1027, naming the dismantlement of scam centers as a key objective to ensure Beijing saw the offensive as a stabilizing measure and did not intervene against it.Geographic proximity likewise bolsters Beijing's hand with Myanmar's junta, and it has applied corresponding pressure to secure the military government's cooperation on joint operations despite connections between militias allied with the junta and the scam industry. Since Operation 1027, China’s anti-scam efforts in Myanmar occurred primarily through junta channels and have run in parallel with the stabilization of the relationship between Myanmar’s military and Beijing. Xi’s June 2026 state visit with Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing was China’s clearest signal yet of normalizing increasingly friendly ties with Myanmar’s military government, which after taking power in a 2021 coup, held sham elections from December 2025 to January 2026. Many countries, including the United States, refuse to recognize the elections given they were not inclusive, transparent, or competitive, so China’s rare recognition of the junta government further compounds its ability to get the junta to act on Beijing’s interests. Still, China lacks an extradition treaty with or a permanent police presence in Myanmar, even though the two countries have conducted joint operational and capacity-building exercises since 2002.Although there have been fewer joint China-Cambodia anti-scam operations than those with Myanmar’s junta, the bilateral levers between Beijing and Phnom Penh are more enmeshed. China has an extradition treaty with Cambodia dating to 1999, which has facilitated the transfers of Chen Zhi, Lu Xiong, and Liu Ren and has maintained a permanent police presence in Cambodia since 2019 through the China-Cambodia Law Enforcement Cooperation Office. Similar to China’s use of gambling as a reason to establish a permanent law enforcement presence in Cambodia, the issue of scams has been leveraged for further cooperation at the highest levels of the bilateral relationship. Wang Yi called for the complete eradication of scam centers when meeting with Hun Manet and launched a 2+2 security dialogue involving foreign ministers and defense ministers from both countries to deepen cooperation on diplomacy, defense, security, and regional affairs. Still, any joint law enforcement operations are reliant on the cooperation of the Cambodian government, which has incentives to protect elite perpetrators and thus has been reluctant towards sharing intelligence about cyber scam networks with other countries. In Laos, China maintains a permanent police presence and has held an extradition treaty with Vientiane since 2002. Chinese police stations along the Laotian shores of the Mekong grew out of joint river patrols launched in 2011, reports point to consistent Chinese police activity in the Golden Triangle SEZ, and private security companies with state ties provide armed protection for the Lao railway. As with Cambodia, high-level ties have recently strengthened: in June 2026, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith met with Xi after launching a permanent 3+3 strategic dialogue with foreign ministers, defense ministers, and law enforcement. Under this framework, both leaders signed a joint statement agreeing to targeted, continuous joint operations to eliminate fraud.China’s use of bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral frameworks to expand its police presence reflects the reality that, despite its extensive influence, it is not a unilateral actor in the region. For all the power asymmetry between China and Southeast Asian states, their relationships remain negotiated. This is best evidenced in the case of She Zhijiang, owner of the Yatai New City scam center and casino in Shwe Kokko, Myanmar. Facing a litany of criminal charges in China and an Interpol arrest request issued by Beijing, She was arrested in Thailand in August 2022. China then sought his return under the two countries’ 1993 extradition treaty, but he was not transferred to China until November 2025, after a three-year legal battle and a competing Cambodian extradition request slowed the process.Of all its Mekong partners, Bangkok has historically exhibited the most resistance towards allowing Chinese police to operate in the country. After it was founded in 2017, LMLECC was viewed by Thailand as a potential risk to national security, and Bangkok was therefore reportedly reluctant to engage in intelligence sharing. Tensions came to a head in February 2025, when Assistant Minister of Public Security Liu Zhongyi, who was dispatched to lead China's response to the Wang Xing kidnapping, was deployed to help establish a bilateral anti-scam center near the Thai-Myanmar border in Mae Sot. Liu's ability to move freely across the border, at times without Thai officials present, prompted criticism in Thailand from members of the public and parliamentary officials. The backlash was significant enough that Liu offered an apology to Thailand’s defense minister for any perceived infringement on Thai sovereignty—a remarkable concession that nonetheless underscored how far operational realities had drifted from normal diplomatic protocol.After the Liu debacle, joint operations continued along the Thai-Myanmar border, through a Thai-Chinese coordination center in Bangkok’s national police headquarters and via LMLECC and other trilateral mechanisms. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Chinese Vice Premier Li Qiang voiced their commitment to enhancing security cooperation on addressing transnational crime syndicates’ efforts at various levels as recently as July 2026, agreeing to establish a new 2+2 dialogue to bring together foreign and defense ministers regularly. Nevertheless, Beijing’s police activity on Thai soil continues to raise sovereignty concerns. Among these encroachments are Beijing’s regular demands that seized devices be repatriated to China rather than being used by local authorities to gather intelligence. In addition, China also pushes for the direct repatriation of Chinese nationals rescued in joint operations directly to China without adequate Thai police screening.3

Washington's Strategy for Addressing Southeast Asia's Scam Economy

While China’s efforts to address Southeast Asia’s scam economy have been focused on joint international crackdowns and on-the-ground offensives, the United States has primarily wielded sanctions, indictments, and asset seizures as central parts of its effort to destabilize the scam industry. The first U.S. government-led actions specifically against scamming came after reports of money lost by Americans targeted by investment scams nearly doubled from $6.9 billion to $12.5 billion between 2020 and 2023. In September 2023, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCen) issued an alert about “pig-butchering” scams run by criminal syndicates out of Southeast Asia.In September 2024, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued its first scam-centered sanctions package against Cambodian businessman and senator Ly Yong Phat, his conglomerate LYP group, and properties including O-Smach Resort along the Thai-Cambodia border. Shortly after these sanctions, prominent Cambodian investigative journalist Mech Dara (whose reporting on Ly’s connection to the scam industry was central to getting him on U.S. radar) was arrested, and the majority of Ly’s linked businesses vanished from Cambodia’s public corporate records. Dara was released by the end of October but has since been detained and targeted locally for his continued exposure of Cambodia’s scam ecosystem.The Treasury Department continued to lead the U.S. response to cyber scams in Southeast Asia throughout early 2025, identifying Cambodia-based Huione Group as a money-laundering institution and sanctioning Myanmar’s Karen National Army (KNA), an EAO, for its role in “facilitating cyber scams that harm American citizens” Following the introduction of two congressional bills in October and December, the Scam Compound Accountability and Mobilization Act (SCAM) and the Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act, respectively, the Treasury Department’s Office for Foreign Asset Control announced the designation of nine targets in Myanmar and ten in Cambodia for facilitating human trafficking and cyber scams targeting U.S. citizens.October 2025 marked a turning point in both the efficacy and scope of U.S. efforts to combat scam operations in Southeast Asia, representing the first cross-departmental campaign. The Justice Department (DOJ) unsealed an indictment against Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi and announced the seizure of $15 billion in assets, while OFAC, in coordination with the United Kingdom, imposed sanctions on 146 targets tied to the Prince Group transnational criminal organization. Although not part of the same announcement, U.S. trade negotiators shortly thereafter gave Cambodia a 90-day window to demonstrate progress on dismantling scam centers as a condition for tariff relief, linking the issue to economic statecraft.Efforts to combat cybercrime across several arms of the U.S. government were then consolidated in November 2025 with the creation of the Scam Center Strike Force. Created to address a “growing threat posed by Chinese organized crime syndicates operating scam centers in Southeast Asia,” the working group has since coordinated efforts among the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia, the DOJ’s Criminal Division, the FBI, and the U.S. Secret Service. The Strike Force has four mandates: seize and disable U.S.-based infrastructure that enables scamming, identify and charge leaders of scam compounds, trace and seize stolen cryptocurrency funds, and prevent further victimization through public education.While China has leveraged its bilateral relationships with Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia, the U.S. bilateral outreach with these countries has been limited. The United States does not recognize Myanmar’s junta government, nor does it cooperate with EAOs on matters of security. Washington also has not engaged in any government-to-government contact with Vientiane regarding cybercrime, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio did broach the subject at the July ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting, where Laotian officials were present. Engagement with Cambodia is the most extensive of the three, although its cooperation is still highly limited. While U.S.-Cambodian relations hit a nadir in 2017 following Prime Minister Hun Sen’s dissolution of his main opposition party, Phnom Penh’s acquiescence to American pressure came alongside somewhat of a rapprochement in bilateral relations, marked by the U.S. lifting its arms embargo and resuming joint military exercises. In March, the National Bank of Cambodia and the U.S. Treasury Department committed to enhanced information sharing with the United States, reactivating a previously dormant channel, but, given the risk it holds in implicating key state officials, it is unlikely the reactivation of the channel will lead to substantial information sharing. During his July 2026 trip to Asia, FBI Director Kash Patel met with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet to discuss joint efforts to combat online scam operations. As is the case with the reactivated financial information sharing mechanism, outcomes are likely to be limited and selective , but the bilateral conversation nonetheless demonstrates that the U.S. continues to be able to extract verbal commitments from Phnom Penh to crack down on its scam industry.On that same trip to Asia, Patel met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Chiravirakul to deepen cooperation on tackling transnational crime, thanking Bangkok for its role in combatting scam networks. A treaty ally and one of Washington’s closest partners in Southeast Asia, Thailand’s cooperation has played a role in enhancing the evidence that U.S. law enforcement has access to, enabling the United States to issue arrest warrants for key criminal actors. This is thanks in part to expanded access to intelligence gained from American law enforcement embedded in the Royal Thai Police War Room. One substantial trove of intelligence that the United States was able to gain access to through this partnership came from a November raid of the Shunda scam compound in Min Let Pan, Myanmar, by the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA), an EAO. While the freed Chinese nationals were repatriated, 8,000 phones and 1,500 computers were handed over to Thai law enforcement, which, in turn, gave the United States access to the devices. This joint effort provided U.S. law enforcement with the intelligence needed to charge Chinese nationals Huang Xing Shan and Jiang Wei, who managed the Shunda Park compound, with wire fraud conspiracy. In a significant step toward recognizing the role EAOs have and can continue to play in disabling and gathering intelligence from scam operations, the indictment highlighted the central role of the KNLA in the raid. Thailand’s cooperation with the United States has also played a key role in opening space for multilateral operations like the one conducted with China, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates in Dubai.4

Misaligned Incentives and Structural Challenges Limiting U.S.-China Coordination

Several obstacles and risks have thus far prevented U.S.-China coordination on addressing Southeast Asia’s scam economy, all of which are underpinned by a deep distrust between the two countries. One such point of friction is Washington’s wariness of Beijing’s leveraging the threat of cyber-scam proliferation to grow the presence of China’s Global Security Initiative. China’s use of bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral partnerships to crack down on scams has enabled it to rapidly expand its security footprint in Southeast Asia, to which U.S. government officials have sounded the alarm: a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission report, originally published in July 2025 and updated in March 2026, concluded that China was “exploiting” the growing crisis of scam centers to build its political influence in Southeast Asia and beyond.Beyond amplifying intelligence-sharing and operational agreements with regional partners, China has capitalized on its cyber-scam offensive to enhance its on-the-ground surveillance capacity across Southeast Asia—both through MPS channels and by leveraging China’s private sector. In Bangkok, Huawei has installed a city-wide surveillance grid. In Laos, Chinese companies have built out the Lao Ministry of Public Security’s internet infrastructure used by local police to combat cybercrime. The proliferation of Chinese surveillance methods and the regulatory opacity surrounding them is central to U.S. concerns over the expansion of China’s security state. Cooperation with Beijing that involves the expansion of Chinese-led surveillance via infrastructure, or an expanded police presence carries the risk of enhanced political policing of overseas Chinese populations and minority communities abroad.While the April 2025 operation in Dubai proved that joint raids involving Beijing and Washington are possible, it remains unclear what happens after one. Intelligence is a sharp point of friction because the information that both enables and is obtained from raids of scam compounds is precisely the kind neither side trusts the other to hold. Devices seized in these operations are intelligence troves: they contain victims’ financial records and identity documents alongside evidence of the syndicates’ internal operations. This critical evidence includes money flows, protection arrangements, and communications that may implicate politically connected figures.Neither the United States nor China has any incentive to let the other see this material. For Washington, the prospect of Chinese state access to the personal and financial data of hundreds of thousands of American fraud victims represents a counterintelligence risk. For Beijing, seized devices may expose connections between criminal networks and Chinese state-linked actors. China has historically treated digital forensics as a unilateral enterprise, hauling confiscated computers and phones back across the border for processing and declining to share the resulting intelligence with other actors involved in joint raids on scam centers. Given that China has consistently withheld intelligence from closer partners, it is highly unlikely that Beijing will be willing to give Washington access without receiving something in return.High-level operators themselves are troves of intelligence that could be useful for future law enforcement efforts. For this same reason, China is unlikely to cede any high-level Chinese nationals to the United States should there be contradicting indictments or extradition requests. For example, Chen Zhi’s extradition to China was likely initiated in such close succession to the announcement of U.S. charges to ensure that Chen never made it to an American courtroom. The United States and China likewise diverge on how low-level scam center operators, often victims of trafficking, should be processed. While tens of thousands of Chinese nationals have been removed from scam compounds and repatriated to China, the Chinese government has only published a few isolated cases in which scammers were classified as victims of trafficking. Experts on transnational crime and other human rights advocates have called for the Chinese government to increase transparency about the victim identification process for those repatriated from the compounds. Working with Beijing on joint raids carries the risk of involuntary repatriation and prosecution of trafficked workers from China, which runs counter to the U.S.’ longstanding assertion that victims of trafficking should not be held criminally responsible for their involvement in unlawful activities that are a direct result of their victimization.Any account of U.S.-China misalignment on scam compound enforcement is incomplete without treating host-state political economy as a core explanatory variable. In Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos, scam operations are not simply tolerated by weak states but are embedded in the revenue streams and patronage networks of governing elites. Because host governments derive material benefit from scam compounds, they face incentives to manage external pressure rather than eliminate its source, and strategic distrust between the United States and China gives them the means to do so. For example, when Washington escalated pressure on Myanmar's junta to crack down on scam compounds in Myawaddy, the junta sacrificed the most expendable part of the problem, arresting 2,198 low-level operators from the KK Park complex while protecting affiliated militia leaders and criminal elites. Then, the junta dismissed U.S. concern over the industry with claims that the rising pressure from Washington concealed a "hidden agenda" and amounted to meddling in Myanmar's internal affairs—something that the junta knew would inevitably spark concern from Beijing. The result is that U.S. and Chinese efforts, even where their objectives overlap, are often weakened by host state strategies that convert great power competition into regime protection.Above all, the deepest misalignment preventing the U.S. and China from coordinating anti-scam efforts is fundamental: each country is incentivized to protect its own citizens first. China’s crackdowns on scam centers in Southeast Asia have concentrated on operations targeting Chinese nationals, not those preying on Westerners or victims elsewhere. Thus, after Beijing intensified enforcement in 2023, syndicates pivoted from targeting Mandarin speakers to targeting English speakers, sparking concerns from some in Washington about Beijing strategically cracking down on scam centers to amplify the industry’s impact on Americans.However, it is this whack-a-mole nature of the scam industry that makes a clear case for cooperation. If enforcement remains nationally siloed, syndicates will simply redirect their operations toward victims in regions where anti-scam enforcement is weakest. Given the extent of China’s scam crackdown, transnational criminal syndicates may have pivoted toward targeting Westerners; but as soon as Chinese officials take their foot off the pedal, crime syndicates will shift back to targeting the Mandarin-speaking world. The Chinese government is currently funneling an immense amount of operational capacity into this issue, but it cannot afford to give it this amount of attention forever, especially as the industry evolves with AI and expands to regions where China has less of an established security presence.Both the United States and China have intelligence that the other party needs: the United States cannot map the syndicates’ China-facing infrastructure, and China cannot see the dollar-denominated financial flows that U.S. investigators are best positioned to trace. While the United States has had success in seizing stolen funds—most notably the $15 billion confiscated in Chen Zhi’s indictment—the U.S. Attorney’s Office has indicated that it is having serious challenges figuring out to whom the money belongs. Money laundering from scams is often routed through PRC-based shadow banking systems, meaning that China holds financial information critical to tracing how laundered funds change hands.The impact of U.S. and Chinese pressure on the Cambodian government to crack down on its scam economy is evidence that parallel pressure is effective. The April 2026 raid in Dubai is proof that tactical law enforcement is possible, and the readout from FBI Director Kash Patel’s July 2026 visit to Beijing indicates that there appears to be interest in cooperation at the ministerial level. The question is now how to move beyond platitudes, ensure that the Dubai joint raid is not a one-off instance of cooperation, and engage in strategic and bounded coordination that takes into account the misaligned incentives and obstacles described in this section.

Policy Recommendations

Given Washington’s strategic interest in working with Beijing to combat Southeast Asia’s scam economy, the following section outlines a framework to broach tactical and bounded law enforcement coordination. These recommendations draw from an understanding of what motivates Beijing’s actions against cybercrime and its crackdown strategy, and where Washington’s and Beijing’s approaches align and diverge. Furthermore, the relative success of fentanyl negotiations between the United States and China offers an important reference point for tactical cooperation on a deeply politicized issue. While issues of cyber-scam centers and the transnational drug trade are fundamentally different and should be handled accordingly, there are certain valuable elements for U.S. policymakers to take into consideration.Push for Leader-to-Leader Engagement on Cyber ScamsThe combination of closed-door pressure on the Chinese government and continued investigations into potential connections between the scam industry and the Chinese state is perhaps the most important element influencing the likelihood of any future U.S.-China cooperation. As with cooperation on fentanyl, progress will be made at the leader-to-leader level, and at least two more meetings between Xi and Trump are expected in 2026. FBI Director Patel’s November and July visits to Beijing are evidence that conversations about joint operations have occurred at the ministerial level, but elevating discussions at the highest levels beyond superficial mentions of the issue should be a priority.The U.S. campaign to force fentanyl onto the bilateral agenda offers an instructive parallel. Washington deliberately raised the reputational cost of Beijing's inaction on its precursor chemical industry, deploying unsealed indictments against Chinese nationals, targeted sanctions packages, and sustained public exposure of China's outbound drug trade. That playbook—pressure through publicity and backed by legal and financial tools—translates readily to the transboundary challenge posed by the scam industry. There are two key differences, however. First, unlike fentanyl, those affected by scamming are not just Americans: Chinese citizens are also major victims. Second, Beijing is already conducting a visible crackdown on the scam ecosystem in Southeast Asia. External pressure, therefore, should target the gaps in that campaign rather than its existence. Continued analysis of the shortcomings of China's anti-scam strategy, alongside research into ties between high-level criminal actors and the party-state (such as the U.S. Select Committee on China's May report on links between the CCP and the cybercrime industry) can help elevate the issue in bilateral negotiations. However, this analysis must remain measured rather than politicized, as excessive finger-pointing risks shifting the focus from the criminal syndicate leaders to a U.S.-China blame contest.Prior to any leader-to-leader negotiations, the White House will have to determine exactly where addressing cyber scams falls on its list of priorities. Progress on the fentanyl issue was made by pulling other levers, including a reduction in the fentanyl-related tariff, suspension of port fees, and an extension of the trade truce. Given China’s relative advantage in terms of intelligence-gathering methods and operational capacity, broader bilateral cooperation on cyber scams from China will, like fentanyl, likely require certain U.S. concessions. The following recommendations offer a starting point for some of the asks that can be made in these meetings, but the United States needs to be clear on what exactly it wants to avoid rhetorical platitudes that produce limited tangible progress.Use Third Parties as IntermediariesCurrently, the United States and China have neither the institutional infrastructure nor the diplomatic trust needed to advance bilateral law enforcement operations. Thus, the engagement of other countries as mediators will be essential to any coordination of joint operations. The success of the Dubai raids can be attributed in part to the roles of Thailand and the United Arab Emirates to streamline intelligence gathering and operational details, allowing both the United States and China to contribute without liaising through bilateral channels. While Beijing has historically shown a preference for bilateral diplomacy, its use of multilateral and trilateral frameworks to address the cyber-scam epidemic in Southeast Asia is evidence of its willingness to engage with such frameworks with agreeable terms.In early July, Thailand launched SHIELD, the first platform designed specifically to integrate intelligence targeting transnational scams and human trafficking. The system enables participating agencies to exchange real-time information on scam compound locations, criminal financial networks, suspected offenders, and trafficking victims, helping authorities coordinate investigations, rescue operations, and cross-border enforcement more efficiently. Importantly, it positions Thailand in the middle of intelligence brokerage, allowing it to formalize the coordination it has carried out previously through several bilateral and multilateral channels. The framework also has the potential to strengthen Thailand’s ability to steer the intelligence narrative and prevent China from seizing devices and valuable data during joint raids. To date, Thai police report that SHIELD has already been adopted by partners in ten countries, including China and the United States, and has immense potential as an asset in future bilateral cooperation between the two.Similarly, empowering third parties such as Thailand to manage intelligence could ultimately translate into a related role of transferring custody of arrested suspects after raids, as Dubai police did in April. As scam centers proliferate out of Southeast Asia and are increasingly staffed with non-Chinese actors, transferring custody of those arrested in raids may become easier to coordinate as China has less reputational damage at risk. The Dubai raid is likely an example of this demographic shift: Beijing has not published any repatriation numbers, and given the frequency with which the Chinese government publicizes successful metrics from its scam crackdowns, likely indicates that the 276 arrested were mostly not Chinese nationals.Broadening partnerships into multilateral arrangements has the potential to be even more effective than focusing on trilateral cooperation, diffusing the pressure on any single intermediary by empowering participants that are neither American nor Chinese. Candidates include countries into which the industry is already expanding, such as Sri Lanka, Indonesia, and parts of West Africa, as well as those with intelligence to share and strong anti-scam mandates of their own, such as Singapore, South Korea, and the Philippines. In operations related to cracking down on scams in Sri Lanka, India would likely get involved given its outsized influence on the island nation. As Washington has strong intelligence-sharing practices with New Delhi, this could give the United States a leg up in any multilateral operation involving the three countries and China.There is also room for regional and international bodies to bridge the gap between Washington and Beijing. ASEAN is one candidate. As Singapore, which has conducted a robust countrywide initiative to prevent its own citizens from being scammed, prepares to chair ASEAN in 2028, it should consider the role that the organization can play in coordinating cooperation between Washington and Beijing. Interpol, of which both the United States and China are members, likewise has the established capacity to coordinate intelligence sharing and joint operations among countries conducting anti-scam offensives and already has two units working on cybercrime. These units helped coordinate Operation First Light, a Chinese-funded global anti-fraud operation that led to the arrest of 5,811 individuals and the interception of $293 million in illicit assets between January and April 2026. While conversations with Interpol officials suggest that both the United States and China have historically been reluctant to share information through their channels, the United States did not participate in Operation First Light.Approach China with IntelligenceA critical imbalance in intelligence distribution related to cyber scams exists between the United States and China. While the United States has benefited from access to devices collected by Thailand within the past six months, China has collected massive troves of both human and digital intelligence since it began cracking down on the scam industry in 2023. Given Beijing’s history of refusing to share intelligence on perpetrators with international law enforcement, Beijing will be in no rush to provide this information. If the United States wants to gain access to it, it will need to come to China with intelligence about scam operations to which China does not already have access.As the scam industry expands its footprint into countries where China has less of a security presence, the United States may gain a growing advantage in intelligence access that China seeks about its own nationals—particularly by leveraging intelligence partnerships with countries where China lacks strong ties. The Philippines has access to a large amount of intelligence from devices seized from crackdowns on online gambling operations known as POGOS (Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators) that proliferated between 2012 and 2019. It is in Washington’s interest to help Manila process and analyze this data, especially since it might contain information about Chinese actors of interest to Beijing. Like Phnom Penh, Manila will likely have concerns about what the information might reveal about host-state corruption, but Washington has the political capital it needs to get the Philippines to share intelligence that it does not necessarily have with Cambodia.A vast amount of intelligence can be gathered from the thousands of non-Chinese scam workers freed in Cambodia's 2026 crackdown. Cambodian officials report that some 200,000 workers from 35 countries have been released, and, while China has hastily processed repatriations of its nationals, thousands of others remain stranded in Cambodia awaiting return to their home countries. These workers hold detailed knowledge of scam centers' internal operations, ownership structures, and where the industry is pivoting in response to the crackdown. Such testimony has already proven its value: OFAC's April 2026 designation of Cambodian Senator Kok An and 28 individuals and entities in his network cited reports from individuals held at facilities run by the K99 Group, a network affiliate. Notably, the most detailed public accounting of K99's operations was facilitated by a Vietnamese non-profit that helped rescue trafficked workers, not by the Cambodian government. Given the sensitivity of what these workers can reveal about the industry's connections to Cambodian elites, Phnom Penh is unlikely to make the thousands of recently released workers available for debriefing. The United States should therefore partner with the non-governmental organizations already working with this population, pairing repatriation and humanitarian support with voluntary interviews, to capture intelligence that neither the Cambodian government will readily offer nor China is likely to have.The United States also commands a category of intelligence leverage that China does not: data that illuminates the dollar-denominated layer of the scam economy. Some of this data the U.S. government touches directly through its influence over dollar clearing and the correspondent banking system, while other data sits with U.S.-based and regulated private actors such as blockchain analytics firms, cryptocurrency exchanges, and stablecoin issuers. Tether, for example, is a stablecoin issuer domiciled within reach of the U.S. legal process and has repeatedly cooperated with the DOJ and OFAC to freeze assets tied to “pig-butchering” operations. Like Beijing has information about PRC-based shadow banking systems and RMB-denominated transfers via apps like WeChat, the United States has access to valuable financial information that can be an asset in any negotiation over intelligence sharing.Several other private sector companies based in the United States have working relationships with the U.S. government and have access to data that might be important to the Chinese government’s anti-scam efforts. Like WeChat is for China, Meta’s platforms remain the primary communication channel between scam syndicates and their victims in the Western world, providing the company visibility into the fake account networks, advertising infrastructure, and recruitment channels through which compounds source both targets and trafficked workers. Likewise, Starlink’s terminal geolocation data offers a near-real-time map of compound activity in ungoverned areas of Myanmar, for which the DOJ has already issued seizure warrants. Because this data maps directly onto Beijing’s own enforcement priorities, Washington can and should engage with U.S.-based companies that China might have an interest in, although user privacy needs to be a central consideration in any such conversations.Above all, to both support the intelligence gathering needed to facilitate coordination with Beijing and bolster its approach to combating the scam economy, the United States needs to invest in and protect civil society who have generated much of the evidence behind U.S. enforcement actions against transnational crime in Southeast Asia. Reporting from Radio Free Asia, which has been defunded by the Trump administration, was critical to building international scrutiny of Chen Zhi and the Prince Group’s activities. A 2024 study by what was formerly known as the U.S. Institute of Peace, an organization whose funding was also cut by the Trump administration, was likewise critical in bringing the U.S. government’s attention to the size of the scam industry in Southeast Asia. Beyond funding these institutions, the U.S. should prioritize the protection of actors on the ground in Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar who have generated much of the evidence needed to make U.S. sanctions and indictments possible. Journalists, frontline providers, labor advocates, local investigators, and technical researchers have been subject to monitoring, intimidation, and arrests for their documentation work that substantially benefits the U.S. anti-scam strategy. Support for these actors and funding for these institutions should be considered essential to the work of the Scam Center Strike Force and broader U.S. national security. Currently, it is not.Leverage Existing Channels for Financial Intelligence SharingInstead of exploring new channels through which to share financial intelligence with China, the United States should build on anti–money laundering and intelligence-sharing platforms that already exist. In 2015, under the Obama administration, FinCEN and the China Anti-Money Laundering Monitoring and Analysis Center (CAMLMAC) signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) establishing a framework for exchanging financial intelligence. Because China does not share information about financial crimes and money laundering through the Egmont Group, no formal channel for such exchanges between the United States and China existed before the MOU was signed. Yet neither FinCEN nor the Treasury Department has publicly reported any exchanges, cases, or joint products under the MOU since its signing, indicating that it was never meaningfully activated.This does not mean there has been no financial intelligence sharing between Washington and Beijing since 2015. Cooperation on the flow of fentanyl and other synthetic opioids and their precursors is one instance of ad hoc coordination, enabled in part by the creation of a counternarcotics working group that made anti-money-laundering coordination a standing agenda item. The working group was an important step, and a parallel body should be created to coordinate action against cyber scams. But it is a high-level policy dialogue, not an operational information-sharing mechanism: it convenes senior officials at random intervals, its agenda is set through diplomatic negotiation, and its continuity depends on the overall state of the bilateral relationship. A dialogue of this kind can signal political commitment and unblock cooperation, but it cannot process case-level financial data on the timelines that money-laundering investigations require. Activating the FinCEN-CAMLMAC channel to track money laundering tied to scam operations would fill that operational gap. It could be leveraged on a case-by-case basis to flag suspicious flows tied to compounds without either side needing to hand over sources or methods. Because it operates below the political level, it would be less exposed to the fluctuations in the bilateral relationship that have repeatedly interrupted higher-profile cooperation.Incentivize China to Continue Extraditing Key ActorsWhile sharing databases of wanted figures would enable the United States and China to combine their economic and operational efforts to weaken and extradite key scammers, this degree of cooperation is politically unrealistic at the current moment. Sanctions packages are highly guarded before they are released to prevent targets from moving their money, and it is difficult to imagine the United States giving China forewarning of the seizure of assets of a Chinese citizen, even one wanted by MPS, in the current political environment.What the United States can and should continue to do is incentivize Beijing to extradite actors through sanctions and indictments that raise the political and reputational cost of inaction. Unless the United States can issue an extradition request in a country with which it has strong ties, it is unlikely that U.S.-initiated extradition requests for Chinese nationals will be granted in countries with strong ties to China.5However, when backed by strong intelligence and maximum public exposure, it appears that U.S. enforcement actions can help catalyze parallel efforts by Beijing to extradite a high-level actor, as it did with Chen Zhi. Thus, if the United States possesses the intelligence needed to indict or sanction a high-level criminal actor involved in scam operations, it should act swiftly and do so in a high-profile manner.There are ways for the United States to preview those Beijing wants to take into custody without the existence of a joint target list. Since late 2023, China’s MPS has issued wanted notices naming individual scam-network figures it wants returned to China, including high-level operators such as Myanmar’s Four Families. Washington can strategically leverage this information to identify where interests align and sequence enforcement actions accordingly, as cases that overlap are more likely to translate into an arrest or prosecution. However, China does not publicly release all the names of actors it wants to take into custody, especially in cases such as Chen Zhi’s, where targets are considered politically sensitive. Public signals alone, therefore, are an incomplete guide to where interests align; when the United States pursues an actor whose name China has not made public, it should anticipate competing extradition requests.

Conclusion

Combatting the cybercrime industry in Southeast Asia represents a rare moment of mutual interest for both the United States and China, although the two have approached it differently. While Beijing has leveraged bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral frameworks to facilitate joint on-the-ground operations and the mass repatriations of Chinese nationals, the United States has primarily wielded sanctions, indictments, and asset seizures. The two approaches have at times complemented each other, as evidenced by the pressure that incited the Cambodian government’s current crackdown, but the absence of cooperation has allowed the industry to proliferate in Southeast Asia and beyond.Concerns about China’s GSI expansion, intelligence sharing sensitivities, host-state political economies, and Beijing’s treatment of trafficked workers are substantial obstacles that have stood in the way of any coordination on the issue of cyber scams beyond the April raid in Dubai. These trust deficiencies and misaligned incentives should not be ignored in favor of naive cooperation but rather factored into how Washington engages with Beijing on future law enforcement operations. The recommendations section provides a framework for such tactical coordination, as does it recognize that connections between the party-state and criminal actors should continue to be researched, though this should not predicate the fact that Beijing has exhibited a legitimate interest in and effort toward addressing cyber scams that target Chinese nationals. The main drivers behind Chinese actions—domestic pressure, reputational damage, and threats to national security—will continue to fuel its response, and it is in Washington’s interest to determine where and how it can engage with Beijing tactically on this issue. As the case of fentanyl showed, even narrow cooperation benefits the broader relationship, and the recommendations outlined in this paper offer a starting point in light of misaligned incentives and strategic rivalries.As the industry evolves with the use of AI and spreads beyond Southeast Asia, the United States and China have an important window to push for joint law enforcement coordination against the scam industry. While FBI Director Kash Patel’s visit to Beijing in July was a step toward elevating the issue of cyber scams prior to President Xi’s trip to the United States in September, policymakers in Washington should continue to push for the topic’s inclusion on the summit’s agenda, as well as for subsequent bilaterals should Trump and Xi meet on the sidelines of APEC and the G20 later this year. U.S. law enforcement should also leverage the frequency of leader-to-leader meetings this year to expedite partnership with China for trilateral or multilateral operations against scam centers. A joint operation prior to September’s meeting can help express goodwill going into upcoming meetings just as the Dubai raid did.The author would like to thank Meredith Foster for her research assistance; Juliet Lee, Emma Chanlett-Avery, Debra Eisenman, and Lyle Morris for their review and edits; Jacob Sims for his expert insights and guidance; and Morgan Speece for her support.
